label: Saddle Creek
description: Hop Along's third Saddle Creek album adds string arrangements and more elaborate production to the band's yelping, emotionally raw songwriting, widening its scope without losing Frances Quinlan's idiosyncratic phrasing. It is the most polished Hop Along record, and the closest the band gets to the anthemic, full-band scale that defines the wider Core sound.
lineage: Third full-length; extends the emo-to-indie-rock arc Hop Along shares with other Philadelphia-scene Core bands like Slaughter Beach, Dog.

label: Good English Records
description: This Austin trio led by songwriter and guitarist Jamie Weed makes its debut LP a collaborative, cathartic mix of '90s alternative dynamics, 2010s emo phrasing, and pedal-tinged bedroom folk. Terry described it as embracing pain fearlessly, running toward heartbreak rather than away from it, across jams that build from hushed verses to full-band peaks.
lineage: New Austin band signed to Good English Records; part of the same emo-into-twang wave as Cusp and Twine, but with a more explicitly folk-pedal-steel palette.

label: Self-released
description: A nine-song set built around memorable, unfussy melodies and a rotating cast of guest vocalists, giving these hushed folk songs a communal, porch-session feel rather than a solo-singer-songwriter one.
lineage: Continues the plainspoken small-town folk of Old Friend with a wider circle of collaborators, part of the 2020s wave of Bandcamp-first indie-folk acts Josh Terry has tracked at No Expectations.

label: No Quarter
description: Recorded in a friend's upstate New York barn, this is spare, unhurried folk built from a repeating image of a bird hitting a window; Horn's guitarist trades quiet call-and-response lines with her plainspoken vocal across ten dreamlike songs.
lineage: Grew out of Horn's Austin songwriting circle and a period studying poetry; No Quarter also houses Joan Shelley, placing Horn in the same lineage of hushed, literary indie folk.

label: Self-released
description: Horn's self-titled follow-up is minimalist to the point of near-silence in places, sparse guitar figures under scalpel-precise, evocative lyric fragments; a dreamy, unhurried record that rewards close listening.
lineage: A further distillation of the hushed, literary style she developed on The Window Is The Dream.

album: It's Summer, I Love You, and I'm Surrounded by Snow
label: Self-released
description: Geneviève Beaudoin's twelve-song set swings her voice from a warble to a coo to a full scream over dark, romantic, disorienting folk arrangements; a breakup and self-reckoning record that never settles into one register for long.
lineage: Part of the Portland, Maine DIY folk scene alongside Lily Seabird's circle; Terry compared the impact of Beaudoin's voice here to first hearing Angel Olsen's Burn Your Fire.

label: Fat Possum Records
description: A love record shadowed by quiet anxiety, veering from insular early Hand Habits songwriting toward a fuzzier, 90s-indebted guitar-rock feel in the vein of Aimee Mann or Neko Case, with occasional horns and Wurlitzer.
lineage: Follows Fun House's move outward from Duffy's solo bedroom style, made as Duffy also became a full-time member of Perfume Genius's touring band.

label: Self-released
description: A Seattle bassist-singer's rich, lush-voiced solo debut of organically arranged folk songs, quiet and confident in its plainspoken storytelling.
lineage: Blackwell is primarily a bassist and guitarist in the Seattle scene; My Maze established her as a songwriter in her own right before Dream a Day.

label: Self-released
description: Ten warm, unhurried songs continuing Blackwell's plainspoken songwriting, self-released between her debut and the more widely noticed Dream a Day.
lineage: A bridge record between My Maze and Dream a Day, part of Blackwell's steady, independent Bandcamp release schedule.

label: Self-released
description: A rich, lush-voiced set of thirteen organically arranged folk songs, self-released only on Bandcamp; Blackwell's most fully realized record to date.
lineage: The culmination of Blackwell's run of independent Seattle folk records, released as her profile grew beyond her session-musician reputation.

album: I Need to Start a Garden
label: Mama Bird Recording Co.
description: Heynderickx's debut is conversational, fingerpicked folk that finds grace in the mundane, from housework to horticulture, sung in a voice that can turn from a murmur to a full-throated cry within a verse.
lineage: Emerged from Portland's DIY folk circuit; the record's patient, plainspoken observation set a template picked up by later Mama Bird and Fat Possum-adjacent songwriters like Lily Seabird.

label: Mama Bird Recording Co.
description: Ten verdant, conversational songs continuing the plainspoken observation of her debut, finding quiet grace in ordinary domestic and natural detail across a patient, guitar-centered record.
lineage: A six-years-later follow-up to I Need to Start a Garden, made after Heynderickx spent the interim touring and collaborating, including on the Max García Conover duo record.

label: Fat Possum Records
description: A duo record rooted in Woody Guthrie and radical folk history, nuanced protest songs traded between two plainspoken, patient singer-guitarists.
lineage: Connects Heynderickx's Portland folk lineage to Maine songwriter Max García Conover's own Woody Guthrie-indebted catalog.

label: Transgressive / Liberation / Polyvinyl
description: Jacklin's debut pairs a plainspoken alto with spare, twang-tinged arrangements, coming-of-age songs about leaving small-town New South Wales that sit closer to country-folk than to polished pop.
lineage: Grew from Melbourne's singer-songwriter scene; set up the more countryish overlap with Core sound that would surface fully on Pre Pleasure.

label: Transgressive / Liberation / Polyvinyl
description: A breakup record about bodily autonomy and the end of a long relationship, delivered in Jacklin's plain, unadorned voice over spare full-band arrangements that lean acoustic more than electric.
lineage: Widely cited alongside Maple Glider and Stella Donnelly as part of a wave of Australian songwriters mining plainspoken, folk-rooted heartbreak writing.

label: Transgressive / Liberation / Polyvinyl
description: Jacklin's most overtly twang-inflected record, with clean electric guitar and horns wrapped around wry, closely observed songs about love, faith and self-image.
lineage: The clearest overlap between Jacklin's pop-folk songwriting and Core's twangy indie-folk sound, cited by Terry alongside Maple Glider's I Get Into Trouble as a touchstone.

album: Now Would Be A Good Time
label: Jagjaguwar
description: Three former high-school friends trade dazzling three-part harmonies over acoustic-led arrangements, wry and darkly funny songs about breakups, dissociation and modern early-twenties life.
lineage: Signed to Jagjaguwar (Bon Iver, Angel Olsen, Sharon Van Etten), the trio toured with Julia Jacklin and sit close to her and Stella Donnelly in the current Australian indie-folk wave.

label: Consonant Records
description: Cornfield's early full-band folk-rock record, plainspoken road-life songwriting delivered in her low, conversational alto.
lineage: Part of Cornfield's Montreal/Toronto folk-rock catalog that eventually led to the more widely noticed Could Have Done Anything.

label: Polyvinyl Record Company / Double Double Whammy
description: A patient, plainspoken record made during the pandemic, continuing Cornfield's steady run of low-key, drummer's-ear folk-rock songwriting.
lineage: Sits between The Shape of Your Name and the more widely reviewed Could Have Done Anything.

label: Next Door Records
description: Terry heard the lead single 'You and Me' as feeling 'like a Tom Petty song in the best way'; the LP is Cornfield's most confident and widely noticed record, warm folk-rock built for the road.
lineage: The culmination of Cornfield's steady solo run after years as a touring drummer for other bands.

label: RCA
description: Marten's teenage debut, hushed and delicately fingerpicked, a precociously assured folk record built around her breathy, unadorned voice.
lineage: Marten came up through YouTube covers and the UK singer-songwriter circuit before signing to RCA; this debut set the hushed template she has expanded over five albums.

label: RCA
description: A slightly fuller-band second album than the debut, still built around Marten's hushed, breathy delivery and fingerstyle guitar, with subtly more textured production and a touch more low-end warmth in the arrangements.
lineage: Continues the debut's hushed folk approach before Marten's move to Fiction Records for Flora Fauna.

label: Fiction
description: A newly confident, full-band-driven record made after a period of writer's block, warmer and more rhythmically alive than her first two RCA albums.
lineage: Marks Marten's move from RCA to Fiction and a fuller, more grounded folk-pop sound.

label: Fiction
description: A warm, love-steeped record, softer and more contented in tone than Flora Fauna, still built on Marten's fingerstyle guitar and close vocal harmonies.
lineage: Continues Marten's Fiction-era run toward fuller, twangier folk arrangements ahead of Dog Eared.

label: Fiction
description: Marten's most commanding record, full-band indie folk with twangy melodies and earthy production, a marked step up in scale from her hushed early albums.
lineage: The clearest example yet of Marten's folk songwriting picking up genuine twang texture, per Terry's review.

album: I Keep My Feet on the Fragile Plane
label: Double Double Whammy
description: Quietly contemplative, introspective songwriting dressed with French horn, English horn and pedal steel, produced by Luke Temple; widely praised as a career high point.
lineage: Krieger's writing here drew comparisons across Terry's coverage to the strongest songwriters of her generation, ahead of the following year's Art of the Unseen Infinity Machine.
key_tracks: I Keep My Feet on the Fragile Plane

label: Drag City
description: Pratt's second album, warbling, hazy fingerstyle folk sung in her distinctive high, cracked vibrato, associated with the freak-folk revival but closer in spirit to Vashti Bunyan than to any twang scene.
lineage: Her only album for Drag City between the self-released debut and Mexican Summer's Quiet Signs.

label: Mexican Summer / City Slang
description: A more finely produced, flute- and piano-inflected record, still built on Pratt's warbling voice and fingerstyle guitar but with a warmer, more meditative pace.
lineage: Her Mexican Summer debut, expanding her sound just ahead of Here in the Pitch.

label: ANTI-
description: A more confident, searching second album about a first queer relationship, cut with Logan Chung and Alberto Sewald and featuring a Christian Lee Hutson co-write.
lineage: Continues Kirby's move from Keeled Scales indie folk toward a bigger ANTI- platform.

label: Self-released
description: Released as Erin Rae and the Meanwhiles, a self-released early record of warm, plainspoken country-folk that predates her solo billing.
lineage: An early document of Rae's Nashville scene before Putting On Airs brought her wider attention.

label: Single Lock Records
description: Rae's breakthrough solo debut, warm and searching country-folk that examines faith, sexuality and family with unusual gentleness and directness.
lineage: Signed her to Single Lock Records and set the plainspoken, gospel-tinged style she carried into Lighten Up.

label: No Quarter
description: Shelley's No Quarter debut, patient and unadorned folk songwriting sung in a clear, plain alto over sparse fingerpicked guitar, with occasional light string and horn touches that never crowd the voice.
lineage: Her first record for No Quarter, the label she'd stay with through Real Warmth, part of the Louisville folk scene alongside Nathan Salsburg.

label: No Quarter
description: A quietly assured second No Quarter record, continuing Shelley's plainspoken, guitar-and-voice folk songwriting with a warmer, more settled tone than the debut and subtle full-band shading.
lineage: Bridges Electric Ursa and her self-titled 2017 breakthrough.

label: No Quarter
description: Shelley's self-titled record, produced with Jeff Tweedy's involvement, widened her audience while keeping the same plain, guitar-and-voice core.
lineage: Her most widely reviewed record before Like the River Loves the Sea, connecting her to the Wilco/Chicago folk-adjacent circle.

label: Revolutions Per Minute
description: A self-released, Bandcamp-only set between her label albums, in the same patient, plainspoken vein as her No Quarter records.
lineage: A stopgap independent release showing Shelley's steady, unhurried songwriting pace.

album: Like the River Loves the Sea
label: No Quarter
description: Recorded in Iceland, a warm and unhurried record continuing Shelley's plain, guitar-centered songwriting with subtly expanded arrangements.
lineage: Follows her self-titled record, keeping her within the No Quarter roster alongside Jana Horn.
key_tracks: Like the River Loves the Sea

label: No Quarter
description: A domestic, duet-filled record made with her husband Nathan Salsburg, continuing Shelley's patient, plain-voiced songwriting.
lineage: Extends the Louisville folk partnership with Salsburg that runs through her whole catalog.

label: No Quarter
description: Lush, lived-in pastoral folk with patient, transcendent songwriting, extending Shelley's decade-plus run of plain, unhurried records.
lineage: Her latest No Quarter album, keeping her among the label's core roster alongside Jana Horn and Bonny Light Horseman.

label: Self-released
description: Sofia Jensen's debut as Free Range: ten tracks of open, subdued, engaging folk begun when she was 15, evoking Elliott Smith, Lomelda and Katy Kirby in its patient, intimate delivery.
lineage: Part of the Chicago DIY folk scene alongside Hannah Frances and Jessica Risker; a quietly confident debut that led directly to Lost & Found.

label: Self-released
description: A subdued, plainspoken second album demanding close attention to Jensen's lyrics, sitting in an Elliott Smith / Adrianne Lenker lane per Terry's review.
lineage: Continues the Chicago DIY folk lineage Jensen established on Practice, now with a fuller and more confident arrangement style.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: Seven mystifying songs pairing the knottiest folk with propulsive energy and a powerful voice, excavating grief over Frances's father's death and years of religious trauma; awarded Best New Music by Pitchfork.
lineage: Frances melds avant-folk, progressive rock and jazz; this record set up her collaboration with Daniel Rossen on Nested in Tangles.

label: Fluff and Gravy Records
description: Southwestern-raised, Portland-based songwriting with Karen Dalton-inspired vocals and psychedelic guitar, plainly indebted to Sandy Denny and country music but bent through indie songwriting.
lineage: Established Valazza in the current wave of country-folk revivalists alongside Erin Rae and Le Ren, ahead of From Newman Street.

label: Fluff and Gravy Records
description: Folk and Americana with wailing pedal steel and introspective lyrics, in the Joni Mitchell / Karen Dalton / Sandy Denny line Terry has traced through Valazza's whole catalog.
lineage: Continues Valazza's country-folk revival songwriting from Knows Nothing with a fuller pedal-steel-driven sound.

label: Bella Union
description: Stratton's sixth album is a hushed, meticulously fingerpicked set that pairs Nick Drake-indebted guitar work with chamber-folk strings. It's patient, literate songwriting built for close listening rather than singalongs.
lineage: Grew from Stratton's decade-plus run as a solo-guitar folk songwriter on Tompkins Square and Bella Union, in the Nick Drake/John Fahey lineage that also runs through Gillian Welch's fingerstyle discipline.

label: Bella Union
description: A widescreen, string-laden folk record named one of the Guardian's best of 2021, pairing Stratton's classical-guitar technique with orchestral arrangements and songs about ecological grief and personal change.
lineage: Continues Stratton's Bella Union run of chamber-folk records descended from Nick Drake and American Primitive guitar playing.

label: Bella Union
description: Stratton's eighth album, praised by Josh Terry as a comparison point for other dusky, tasteful 2025 folk records; continues his classical-guitar-trained, string-accented songwriting.
lineage: Eighth solo album in a Bella Union/Tompkins Square lineage stretching back to his 2007 debut, indebted to Nick Drake and American Primitive fingerstyle guitar.

label: Outside Music
description: Recorded at La Frette studios near Paris, Loyalty is warm, unhurried indie folk with Tamara Lindeman's plainspoken alto out front and light Americana touches (pedal steel, brushed drums).
lineage: Tamara Lindeman's long-running Toronto folk project, moving from 2000s singer-songwriter records toward the more expansive, band-driven indie folk of its 2020s run.
key_tracks: Way It Is, Way It Could Be

label: Outside Music
description: The self-titled fourth album is Lindeman's most purely indie-folk record, eleven wistful, full-band songs about love and self-doubt with jangling guitars and close, conversational vocals.
lineage: Tamara Lindeman's long-running Toronto folk project, moving from 2000s singer-songwriter records toward the more expansive, band-driven indie folk of its 2020s run.

label: Fat Possum
description: A shortlisted Polaris Prize record that folds saxophone, flute and disco-adjacent rhythm into Lindeman's folk songwriting, using climate anxiety as its emotional undertow.
lineage: Tamara Lindeman's long-running Toronto folk project, moving from 2000s singer-songwriter records toward the more expansive, band-driven indie folk of its 2020s run.

album: How Is It That I Should Look at the Stars
label: Next Door Records
description: Written alongside Ignorance but left spare and largely acoustic, this companion album is quieter and more intimate, letting Lindeman's voice and guitar carry most of the weight.
lineage: Tamara Lindeman's long-running Toronto folk project, moving from 2000s singer-songwriter records toward the more expansive, band-driven indie folk of its 2020s run.

label: Fat Possum
description: Longlisted for the 2025 Polaris Prize, Humanhood leans further into improvisation and a loose full-band feel while keeping Lindeman's core folk songwriting intact.
lineage: Tamara Lindeman's long-running Toronto folk project, moving from 2000s singer-songwriter records toward the more expansive, band-driven indie folk of its 2020s run.

label: Ba Da Bing!
description: Hollie Fullbrook's full-band Tiny Ruins record widens the group's hushed, literate folk with warmer full-band arrangements and NZ chart success.
lineage: Grew from Fullbrook's solo Tiny Ruins recordings into a full band that toured with Fleet Foxes and Beach House; part of the same Southern Hemisphere indie-folk lineage as Julia Jacklin and Courtney Barnett's circle.

label: Dear Life Records
description: Hill's debut, recorded live at an Atlanta studio: intricate, self-taught fingerpicking under a plainspoken, nature-fixated songwriting voice indebted to Michael Hurley and Karen Dalton.
lineage: Grew out of Hill's move to the Blue Ridge Mountains and immersion in the American Primitive fingerstyle scene, opening onto her fuller-band later records.

label: Dear Life Records
description: A transitional second record, recorded to 8-track with producer Jason Chronis, that opens Hill's solo fingerstyle sound to a small circle of collaborators including Mat Davidson.
lineage: Follows Azalea as Hill moved back to Austin, expanding her palette ahead of the full-band Hopeful Woman.

label: Dear Life Records
description: Recorded live in Texas and Western North Carolina with Mat Davidson's pedal steel and flute throughout, Hill's third LP is her most fleshed-out, twang-forward record yet.
lineage: Josh Terry flagged it as an album-of-the-year contender for its full-band arrangements; continues Hill's fingerstyle-folk lineage into pedal-steel-laced country-folk.
key_tracks: Blue is the Color of My Sun

label: Thirty Tigers
description: Uwade Akhere's debut full-length after years singing on Fleet Foxes' Shore; a studied, choir-trained voice moves through folk, soul and singer-songwriter modes across nine songs about grief and heritage.
lineage: Grew out of her feature on Fleet Foxes' Shore and years touring as their opener/backing vocalist; part of the same Fleet Foxes-adjacent folk network as Uwade's own Field Guide C5 peers.

label: Self-released
description: A prolific Bandcamp DIY songwriter's tenth-plus full-length, a ten-song set titled in wry homage to AC/DC; lo-fi home recording with a loose, sci-fi-inflected sense of humor.
lineage: Part of the sprawling, self-released Bandcamp DIY-folk scene the field guide places alongside Sleeper's Bell and Hazel City in the Philadelphia/Chicago indie-folk underground.

label: Self-released
description: A nine-song Chicago DIY-folk record, quiet guitar-and-voice arrangements with occasional full-band lift, released with a spring 2025 vinyl pressing.
lineage: Part of Chicago's current Bandcamp indie-folk scene alongside Hazel City and Jessica Risker.

label: Colemine Records
description: Powell's sophomore album, a jazz-inflected folk-rock record carried by her standout voice and a five-piece band of close friends; immaculate, warm instrumental textures throughout.
lineage: Bay Area indie-folk/jazz-folk crossover scene; her voice draws comparisons to classic soul and folk singers alike.

label: Lame-O Records
description: A heart-wrenching, dedicated-to-a-friend record where Lily Seabird's voice swings from a whisper to a shriek over muscular, clanging guitars; Josh Terry wrote its official bio.
lineage: Part of the Burlington, VT scene (Fust, Charlie Hill, Dari Bay) bridging indie folk and full-band rock.

label: Lame-O Records
description: Big-hearted, warm indie rock and folk about finding home and belonging amid chaos, continuing Seabird's mix of hushed verses and full-throated choruses.
lineage: Follow-up to Alas within the Burlington, VT indie-folk/rock scene.

label: Lame-O Records
description: Seabird's fourth LP balances explosive, searing electric guitar passages with quiet, dexterous lead-guitar moments and hushed verses, continuing her run of Lame-O Records albums about home and belonging.
lineage: Fourth album from the Vermont songwriter, continuing the Lame-O Records Burlington-scene run.

label: New West Records
description: Sunny War's breakout, produced by Andrija Tokic, blends folk-punk fingerpicking with gospel, blues and roots textures on 14 tracks about addiction and recovery; David Rawlings and Jim James guest.
lineage: Grew from War's Venice Beach boardwalk busking roots into a full-band Americana sound; part of the same roots-punk lineage as Sadurn and Angel Olsen's early records, per Terry's own comparison.

label: Metropolitan Groove Merchants
description: Donnelly's self-released second album, debuting at No. 29 on the ARIA charts, keeps the wit of her debut while opening into fuller, more atmospheric arrangements.
lineage: Follow-up to Beware of the Dogs, self-released after leaving Secretly Canadian.

label: Dot Dash Recordings
description: Donnelly's third and most introspective album pairs sparse, spacious production with conversational, incisive lyrics and timeless pop-folk melodies, a step back from Flood's fuller arrangements.
lineage: Third album, released via Dot Dash Recordings/Remote Control after two self-directed records.

label: ANTI-
description: Recorded with Mike Mogis in Omaha after signing to ANTI-, Dark Arc pairs the band's dulcimer-and-mandolin folk instrumentation with denser, more electric production.
lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

label: ANTI-
description: A pop-structured folk-rock record built on the band's trademark mix of banjo, dulcimer and balalaika alongside synths and electric guitars.
lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

label: ANTI-
description: An unexpected, innovative folk-rock record per NPR, mixing Appalachian string-band instrumentation with contemporary electronic touches.
lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

label: Lame-O Records
description: Saintseneca's first album in seven years, produced by Steve Ciolek, full of heady surrealist lyrics and rousing, off-kilter earworm hooks.
lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

label: Mare Records
description: Released on Kevin Morby's Mare imprint, Living Water is a spare, Nick Drake-and-Vashti-Bunyan-indebted folk record built on close-mic'd guitar and Lay's airy voice.
lineage: Lay's second solo album, made between stints in the LA punk band Feels; part of the LA cosmic-folk revival around Ty Segall's circle.

label: Sub Pop
description: Lay's first album as a full-time musician and first for Sub Pop, co-produced with Ty Segall and dressed with a wider array of instrumentation than her earlier records.
lineage: Marks Lay's move from Feels' punk records into a dedicated solo folk career.

label: All the Best
description: Lay's fifth album, self-released on her own All the Best label, adds pedal steel, piano and synths to her folk core with a larger team of musicians than before.
lineage: Follows Geist and Covers Vol. 1 as Lay's most expansive solo record to date.

label: Free Dirt Records
description: Produced by Mandolin Orange's Andrew Marlin, Shame is iconoclastic bluegrass-rooted folk with pointed, feminist political songwriting anchored by Baiman's fiddle playing.
lineage: Oak Park, IL-raised fiddler turned Nashville songwriter; part of the same politically engaged old-time/bluegrass-folk lineage as Kara Jackson and Rachel's Folk Fights Back organizing.

label: Signature Sounds Recordings
description: An investigation of generational cycles and inherited pain, delivered through Baiman's old-time-inflected fiddle-and-banjo folk songwriting.
lineage: Third solo record, moving from Free Dirt to Signature Sounds.

label: Signature Sounds Recordings
description: Timeless, justice-minded folk tunes featuring an Erin Rae guest spot and a John Hartford cover, rooted in Baiman's Oak Park upbringing and Nashville old-time scene.
lineage: Continues Baiman's politically engaged Americana songwriting on Signature Sounds.

label: Full Time Hobby
description: Fifteen years after forming, Sam Swinson's band released a debut of dark, twangy country-Americana about addiction, recovery and his upbringing in a religious cult; AllMusic called it 'twangy, sauntering indie rock'.
lineage: Formed in high school in Normal, IL; the band's long hiatus and reunion through recovery gives the record a lived-in country-folk storytelling core close to Wednesday's and Ondara's rural-Midwest lineage.

label: Orindal Records
description: A knotty, dense, patient listen that veers between mesmerizing folk, psych drone and glitchy ambient textures from the former Rodan bassist turned solo songwriter.
lineage: O'Neil's long solo run (Quarterstick, K Records, Kranky) traces from post-rock roots into hushed, experimental indie folk; now on the same Orindal roster as Wednesday.

album: To Enjoy Is the Only Thing
label: Partisan Records
description: Tori Zietsch's debut as Maple Glider, produced by Tom Iansek, takes inspiration from vignettes of her life and travel in spare, intimate folk songs.
lineage: Grew from Zietsch's earlier duo project Seavera into a solo folk career on Pieater/Partisan.

label: Partisan Records
description: Emotionally devastating songs about religion, bodily autonomy and trauma, in the same territory as Julia Jacklin's Pre Pleasure.
lineage: Second album, continuing Maple Glider's confessional Australian indie-folk songwriting.

label: Western Vinyl
description: Billed to Luke Temple and the Cascading Moms, this quiet, falsetto-led folk record continues Temple's Paul Simon/Nick Drake-indebted songwriting outside his Art Feynman and Here We Go Magic projects.
lineage: Longtime Secretly Canadian/Western Vinyl songwriter (Here We Go Magic, Art Feynman) returning to plain solo-folk songwriting.

label: Winspear
description: Lutalo Jones' debut album, recorded at Sonic Ranch with Jake Aron, turns knotty indie rock and warm folk into a bigger, bolder coming-of-age record than their lo-fi Once Now, Then Again EP.
lineage: Vermont multi-hyphenate whose folk-rooted songwriting grew out of the Burlington DIY scene alongside Lily Seabird.

album: Every Time We Turn A Corner
label: Royal Mountain Records
description: Understated, catchy hushed-folk pop across eleven tracks, built on delicate rhythm-section grooves and George Harrison-style slide guitar layered over plainspoken verses.
lineage: Signed to Royal Mountain Records; part of the current wave of hushed-folk-pop songwriters Terry covers alongside Ultra Lights and Proun.
key_tracks: Every Time We Turn A Corner

label: Self-released
description: Nicole Rodriguez's sophomore Pearla album turns from the mysteries of the external world to the interior and relational, sparse omnichord-and-acoustic arrangements framing intimate songs.
lineage: Philadelphia songwriter whose debut was described by Pitchfork as 'a detective of uncertainty'; part of Philly's hushed indie-folk scene alongside Sadurn and Greg Mendez.

label: Northern Spy
description: A dreamworld folk-pop record co-produced with Sam Evian, mixing hushed vocals, vintage guitar tones and bossa nova influence into arrangements Terry compared to a neon-lit western dive bar.
lineage: Argentine-American Brooklyn songwriter whose second Northern Spy album folds bossa nova and folk into a spectral, Timber Timbre-adjacent sound.

label: Run For Cover Records
description: Genevieve DeGroot's full-band debut, recorded in a Poconos cabin during the pandemic; spare, diary-like indie folk indebted to Jason Molina, Gillian Welch and Elliott Smith.
lineage: Grew from DeGroot's lo-fi Philadelphia DIY EPs into a full four-piece band; part of the Philly indie-folk scene alongside Pearla and Greg Mendez.

label: Self-released
description: A raspy-voiced, earthy folk record featuring players from Califone, Megafaun, Mountain Goats and Mountain Man; Nathan Salsburg calls it Moss's best yet.
lineage: New England-born, Virginia-based guitarist whose fingerstyle folk draws on the same Appalachian/American Primitive lineage as Jake Xerxes Fussell.

label: Grand Jury Music
description: Dan Álvarez de Toledo and Jordan Dunn-Pilz's debut LP, twelve songs of finish-each-other's-sentences vocal harmony digging into family history and young-adult self-reflection.
lineage: Childhood-friends duo in the Elliott Smith/Golden Daze songwriting vein; Terry wrote the album's bio.

label: Massif Records
description: Unfussy yet ornate indie folk-rock ranging from stripped melancholy to lush grooves, from the songwriter who also plays bass in Katy Kirby's band.
lineage: Part of the same Brooklyn indie-folk/rock circle as Katy Kirby and Lindsay Reamer.

label: Fire Records
description: Allen's Chris Cohen-produced follow-up to Candlepower is timeless, classic-songwriting-lineage folk anchored by her mesmerizing, wide-ranging voice.
lineage: Los Angeles songwriter whose delicate, literary folk songwriting places her alongside Weyes Blood and Cate Le Bon's circle.

label: Anxiety Blanket Records
description: Buoyant, bittersweet folk-rock built on acoustic guitars, piano and orchestral touches; Terry named 2024's Apple Core as its direct predecessor.
lineage: Los Angeles songwriter drawing '70s-influenced comparisons per The Spill Magazine's review.

label: Orindal Records
description: Friendship's early album stretches Dan Wriggins' plainspoken, funny-sad songwriting over synthesizer, pedal steel and Rhodes piano, mixing live and programmed drums. It is patient, homemade-sounding Americana about work, loneliness and friendship, closer to a whisper than a shout.
lineage: Grew out of Wriggins, Gill and Cormier's shared Philadelphia apartment; the twisted, ambient-pedal-steel take on Americana that defines Friendship's later, more widely heard Merge records starts here.

label: Orindal Records
description: Recorded to tape with The Low Anthem's Jeff Prystowsky, Dreamin' trades Friendship's earlier drum machines for a warmer, more organic sound built on acoustic guitars, soft drums and a haunting pedal steel. Dan Wriggins' lyrics sit in the gap between intimacy and loneliness, sung in a plainspoken near-murmur.
lineage: A bridge between Friendship's rougher early records and the fuller Merge albums to come; shares its unhurried, country-inflected hush with labelmates like Lomelda and hemlock.

label: Merge Records
description: Friendship's second Merge album widens their idea of country music further: shambolic guitars against flute pads, a Motown rhythm section under bleary poetry, and Dan Wriggins' ragged baritone cutting through eleven murky, wry songs. As Josh Terry noted, a song about Jerry Garcia and Betty Ford closes out with a drum solo.
lineage: Continues the slow, twang-inflected songwriting Friendship has refined since 2015, now with more polish and range while staying rooted in the same understated, funny-sad register.

label: Disposable America
description: The Boston trio's self-titled debut sets Will Cashion's deadpan, half-sung vocals over slow, heavy, effects-laden guitar figures. It is a foundational document of the 2010s Boston slowcore-adjacent scene, closer to Duster's hazy drift than to any twang, but decisive for the band's later sound.
lineage: Draws on Duster and Codeine-style slowcore fed through a more melodic, riff-driven Boston indie-rock lens; sets up the run of Run for Cover albums that followed.

label: Run for Cover Records
description: So Divine widens Horse Jumper of Love's palette slightly while keeping their signature slow tempos and heavy-lidded, half-mumbled vocals. Guitars still swell into distorted crescendos, but the songwriting is more direct and melodic than the debut.
lineage: First album for Run for Cover, the label that would house the band through its most acclaimed run; still indebted to Duster/Codeine slowcore.

label: Run for Cover Records
description: Natural Part is a tighter, more focused set of songs than the band's earlier records, still built on Will Cashion's murmured deadpan and slow-burn guitar dynamics. It is a good entry point for the band's core sound of hushed verses breaking into fuzzed-out release.
lineage: Continues the band's Run for Cover run; frequently cited alongside Duster and Bedhead as a reference point for 2020s slowcore revival bands.

label: Run for Cover Records
description: Heartbreak Rules keeps Horse Jumper of Love's slow, weighty tempos while pushing the vocals closer to the front of the mix. It is a moody, unhurried record about heartbreak, delivered with the band's usual dry understatement.
lineage: A steady continuation of the band's Run for Cover-era sound between Natural Part and Disaster Trick.
key_tracks: A Tune Drifts Out the Window

label: Run for Cover Records
description: Disaster Trick was a 2024 favorite Josh Terry left off his year-end list only because he had written the album's press bio; it is another slow, heavy-lidded set of Horse Jumper of Love songs, all murmured vocals and guitars that build toward distorted release.
lineage: The band's most recent full-length, continuing their run for cover as one of the most visible modern slowcore-adjacent groups.

label: Ruination Record Co.
description: Justin Morris's Sluice project turns floating in a North Carolina river into open-hearted, lyrically dense songwriting, loose and lived-in with pastoral, fingerpicked arrangements. It is quiet, plainspoken music about time, faith and place.
lineage: Part of the Durham/Triangle DIY folk-rock circle that also produced Fust and Merge-adjacent bands; Sluice's hushed, country-tinged songwriting feeds directly into the Companion follow-up.

label: Mtn Laurel Recording Co.
description: Companion is weirder and more interior than Radial Gate, recorded with a rotating cast of North Carolina musicians (Libby Rodenbough, Alli Rogers) playing fiddle, Wurlitzer and Echoplex around Justin Morris's plainspoken songs, with room noise and found sound left in the mix.
lineage: A direct sequel to Radial Gate, deepening Sluice's hushed, conversational folk-rock and its ties to the Durham DIY scene.

label: WNOADIARWB
description: Otto Benson's first vocally-focused album is pretty but austere guitar folk, built around a bassy croon and shimmering pedal steel over a sparse palette. Josh Terry called it a quiet accompaniment for navigating the American landscape.
lineage: Emerges from the WNOADIARWB collective's lo-fi/bedroom folk network; its hushed, pedal-steel-laced sound sits alongside Friendship and Lomelda's brand of country-tinged quiet.

label: Dangerbird Records
description: Hataałiinez Wheeler's debut LP as Hataałii is mysterious, hypnotic Arizona indie rock, his deep-voiced surf-country croon set against sparse, slow arrangements. Josh Terry compared his vocal presence to Jim Morrison and Lou Reed.
lineage: First widely-heard record from the Window Rock, Arizona songwriter; establishes the slow, serene surf-country sound he expands on Waiting for a Sign and I'll Be Around.

label: Dangerbird Records
description: Waiting for a Sign is impressionistic and obliquely Nick Cave-like, Hataałii's warbling baritone floating over slow, eerie Americana. Josh Terry called it fit for the Twin Peaks Roadhouse.
lineage: Second Dangerbird Records LP, continuing the hushed, ornate Americana Hataałii built on Singing Into Darkness.

label: Panther Mountain
description: I'll Be Around continues Hataałii's ornate, eerie Americana, a modern crooner's take on heartbreak set over slow, serene surf-country arrangements.
lineage: Third full-length, moving from Dangerbird to the Panther Mountain imprint while keeping the same hushed, baritone-led sound.

label: Self-released
description: Talk Soon is Carolina Chauffe's raw, introspective phone-fi bedroom folk record, stitched together with voicemails from loved ones. Josh Terry called it intimate and homey, a 17-track "interstate phone-fi bedroom folk saga."
lineage: Early, fully self-recorded hemlock LP that establishes the hushed, song-a-day archive Chauffe later reworks into 444; closely tied to Lomelda's Hannah Read, a recurring collaborator.

label: Double Yolk Record House
description: Recorded live as a trio at Lazybones Studio in Silsbee, TX (Lomelda's home base), amen! is a six-song mini-album that gives Carolina Chauffe's solo intimacy full-band urgency, including a Handsome Family cover.
lineage: Bridges hemlock's earlier solo phone-fi work and the full-band 444; recorded in Lomelda's orbit, underlining the Texas/Chicago hushed-folk network this lane draws from.

label: Self-released
description: A surprise release from Newfoundland's Aaron Powell, Midnight Society is quiet, grainy, homespun songwriting that Josh Terry called Fog Lake's most dynamic record, with rockers that recall You Forgot It in People-era Broken Social Scene amid the usual hush.
lineage: Part of Powell's long-running, prolific solo bedroom-folk catalog; a lo-fi Canadian counterpart to the American hushed-twang scene this lane tracks.

label: Captured Tracks
description: Roses is airtight, soaring Widowspeak songwriting with woozy Americana flourishes; Josh Terry singled out its twangy signifiers rather than pure mood-setting, a shift toward the country side of the band's dream-pop sound.
lineage: Part of Widowspeak's later run of quieter, more overtly country-tinged Captured Tracks albums (Plum, Expect the Best, The Jacket), a late-career move toward the C8 sound after starting as dream pop.

label: Dear Life Records
description: The third Little Mazarn album pairs Lindsey Verrill's heart-opening vocals and singing saw with bombastic drums and dissonant synths, recasting the Austin trio's primitive-folk origins into something more expansive. Grief over lost jobs and a parent's death runs through the record.
lineage: Austin's Little Mazarn (featuring hemlock's Carolina Chauffe) sits at the crossroads of the same hushed, Texas-rooted folk network as Lomelda and hemlock, following past LPs Io and Texas River Song.

label: Lima Limo
description: tiarn is delicate, immersive ghostly folk from Melbourne's Hana Stretton, built on spectral harmonies, field recordings and slow, fingerpicked arrangements. Josh Terry described it as folk-ambient at its most hushed.
lineage: A quieter, more ambient-leaning entry in the modern hushed-folk scene this lane tracks, released internationally through Lima Limo (UK) and Inpartmaint (Japan).

label: Topshelf Records
description: Devin McKnight's third Maneka album sits at the combustible intersection of slowcore and shoegaze, alternating quiet, acoustic reflection with head-splitting noise. Engineer Alex Farrar's production keeps the extremes cohesive.
lineage: McKnight (formerly of Speedy Ortiz and Grass Is Green) built Maneka as a showcase for genre-crossing songwriting; this album's slowcore passages place it squarely in this lane alongside Horse Jumper of Love and Joyer.

label: Stray Authority
description: Blanket is hazy, meditative Rochester folk rock that Josh Terry described as pairing gorgeousness with eeriness and wonkiness, its slow tempos and murky production sitting close to the lane's slowcore-adjacent end.
lineage: Follows Shep Treasure's earlier EPs and remix records; vocalist Sabrina Nichols also lends backing vocals to Joyer, tying the two acts to the same East Coast DIY circle.

album: On the Other End of the Line...
label: Julia's War Recordings
description: Brothers Nick and Shane Sullivan dial back Joyer's shoegaze leanings for folkier touches on this LP, recorded with Slow Pulp's Henry Stoehr; pastoral twang runs through cuts like "Cure" and "Glare of the Beer Can" alongside spidery, more explosive rock songs.
lineage: Toured with Horse Jumper of Love and villagerrr; this album's pull toward folk and twang, after a more purely shoegaze-pop prior record, places it at this lane's edge.

label: Sipsman
description: Clifford's second full album swings between pummeling noise and jangle, with moody slowcore passages and a subtle twang running underneath, per Josh Terry's description of the Boston band.
lineage: Part of the same Boston indie-rock underground that produced Horse Jumper of Love, mixing that scene's slowcore heaviness with a lighter, country-tinged jangle.

label: Self-released
description: Teethe's self-titled debut is a self-produced, self-mixed set of slow, hushed Texas indie rock, an early document of the slowcore group that would go on to work with labelmate/collaborator Boone Patrello (Dead Sullivan).
lineage: Grows out of the same Texas DIY-slowcore network as Dead Sullivan; a rawer predecessor to the more polished Magic of the Sale.

label: Self-released
description: A level-up for the Texas slowcore group, Magic of the Sale is dark and enveloping, its nostalgic atmospherics filled out with strings and pedal steel, per Josh Terry's description.
lineage: Teethe's sophomore LP, refining the slow, hushed sound of their self-titled debut with richer, more country-tinged arrangements.

label: Fire Talk Recordings
description: Bnny's debut, written by Jess Viscius across the years after her partner's death, is inky, minimalist noir-pop delivered in a half-whispered voice, drawing on the Velvet Underground's two-chord simplicity for its lo-fi, grief-centered songs.
lineage: The record that established Bnny's hushed, grief-soaked sound, setting up the fuller-band, more shoegaze-inflected One Million Love Songs.

label: Fire Talk Records
description: Bnny's second album is a slowcore/shoegaze/garage record about life after grief, per Josh Terry's framing of its Bandcamp Album of the Day write-up; Jess Viscius's hushed vocals sit over heavier, more fleshed-out arrangements than the debut.
lineage: Continues the grief-driven songwriting of Everything with a fuller, noisier Chicago band sound.

label: Self-released
description: Molly Meehan's debut as vega is gentle, adventurous Burlington indie rock, recorded by Greg Freeman collaborator Cam Gilmour with Hannah Frances guesting. Josh Terry named it one of his favorite records of 2024.
lineage: Part of the Burlington, Vermont DIY scene around Greg Freeman and Hannah Frances that feeds this lane's softer, folk-indebted end.

label: Self-released
description: beacon, how blue pairs nine soft, openhearted, melancholic indie rock songs with woozy twang and waltz-like arrangements, per Josh Terry's description of vega's follow-up to trust me, i'm trying.
lineage: Second vega LP, continuing Molly Meehan's plainspoken, gently twangy Burlington indie-folk songwriting.

label: Orindal Records
description: Little Kid's Orindal Records debut sets Kenny Boothby's urgent, soft-spoken voice against intimate, relentlessly hummable slow-tempo songs with exploratory jazz touches, per Josh Terry's description.
lineage: Toronto songwriter Kenny Boothby's project shares Orindal Records with Friendship and hemlock, part of that label's quiet, folk-leaning slowcore roster.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Recorded in Brussels in April 2003 while the band still toured as Songs: Ohia, this live album was the first release under the Magnolia Electric Co. name. Stretched-out versions of songs like 'The Big Beast' lean hard into Crazy Horse-style guitar jams, with reviewers at the time noting the overt Neil Young worship. It is the document of the exact moment Molina's haunted folk band turned into a loud, loose country-rock outfit.
lineage: Documents Jason Molina's pivot from the hushed Songs: Ohia sound toward Crazy Horse-scale guitar rock, a move that set the template for Magnolia Electric Co.'s studio albums.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Assembled from four separate sessions -- including one produced by Cracker's David Lowery in Richmond and one at Sun Studio in Memphis -- 'Fading Trails' is patchier and more fragmentary than its predecessor, mixing full-band rockers like 'Don't Fade on Me' with short, spare pieces like 'Montgomery'. All of its songs later resurfaced in fuller form on the 'Sojourner' box set. It captures Molina restlessly moving between studios and lineups in the years before Magnolia Electric Co. wound down.
lineage: A transitional Magnolia Electric Co. record whose sessions were later collected whole on the 'Sojourner' box set, showing Molina's late-2000s method of recording in pieces across different studios and bands.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: A limited wooden box set collecting three full albums (including the otherwise-unreleased 'Nashville Moon', produced by Steve Albini), a four-song EP, and a tour documentary, all drawn from the same 2005-2007 sessions that fed 'Fading Trails'. Because it gathers complete, otherwise-hard-to-find recordings rather than just repackaging an existing album, it functions as a genuine (if sprawling) entry in the discography rather than a reissue. It is for the committed listener who wants the full session-by-session picture of Magnolia Electric Co.'s mid-2000s work.
lineage: Collects the same 2005-2007 Magnolia Electric Co. sessions that produced 'Fading Trails' in their entirety, including material otherwise unavailable, and stands as the fullest document of the band's road-band, Crazy Horse-indebted period.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Recorded quickly with Steve Albini as a tribute to Magnolia Electric Co. bassist Evan Farrell, who died in 2009, 'Josephine' is the band's last studio album released in Molina's lifetime. It is quieter and more mournful than the road-band records around it, built on hushed strumming and Molina's weathered voice on songs like the title track and 'Whip-poor-will'. It works as a fitting, restrained close to the Magnolia Electric Co. catalog.
lineage: Closes out Magnolia Electric Co.'s studio catalog as a memorial record for bassist Evan Farrell, recorded just before Molina's final years of illness and his one collaboration with Will Johnson.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: The only proper collaboration between Jason Molina and Will Johnson, recorded together in February 2008 and released the following year, trades the road-band roar of Magnolia Electric Co. for hushed, largely acoustic duets. Songs like 'All Gone, All Gone' and 'The Lily and the Brakeman' put the two songwriters' voices side by side rather than layered into a band mix, with Sarah Jaffe adding backing vocals on one track. It was Molina's last album released before his death in 2013, a quiet capstone to the whole Magnolia/Centro-matic orbit.
lineage: Joins the two central songwriters of the Secretly Canadian/Magnolia orbit -- Jason Molina and Centro-matic's Will Johnson -- directly, making explicit the kinship between Songs: Ohia/Magnolia Electric Co. and the Denton scene.

label: Galaxia
description: A one-off project pairing Jason Molina with Will Oldham and Scotland's Alasdair Roberts, this seven-song EP is plain, unplugged folk balladry, closer to a front-porch song-swap than any of the three writers' main bands. Tracks like 'Maa Bonny Lad' and 'The Gypsy He-Witch' lean on traditional-sounding melodies and close, unpolished harmonies. It is a minor but telling document of how tightly the Molina and Will Oldham/Drag City circles overlapped.
lineage: Directly links Jason Molina to Will Oldham's Drag City deadpan-folk lineage (V2) through a shared acoustic side-project with Alasdair Roberts.

label: Shangri-La Music
description: A studio supergroup pairing Will Johnson's labelmate-adjacent circle with Conor Oberst, Jim James, and M. Ward, 'Monsters of Folk' is a friendly, eclectic indie-folk record that charted in the Billboard Top 20, far more polished and pop-minded than anything in the Molina/Johnson catalog proper. Tracks range from full-band folk-rock ('Say Please') to hushed acoustic duets. It sits closer to 2000s roots-inflected indie than to the Crazy Horse-scale sound of the Magnolia circle.
lineage: Connects Will Johnson to the wider 2000s roots-indie scene around Bright Eyes, My Morning Jacket, and M. Ward, a lighter and more commercial cousin of his work in Centro-matic and with Molina.

label: Steve Records
description: Will Johnson's debut full-length as Centro-matic, recorded and mixed in Denton by Matt Pence, is scrappy, fuzzed-out guitar rock cut fast and cheap, with all twelve songs written and largely performed by Johnson himself. It sounds like a home-recorded garage band with a country streak rather than a polished studio act, closer to lo-fi indie rock than to alt-country proper. It marks the start of the prolific, self-recorded Denton scene that Centro-matic and South San Gabriel would build out over the next two decades.
lineage: Launches Will Johnson's Centro-matic and, with it, the Denton, Texas wing of the Molina/Magnolia orbit; Matt Pence's home-studio methods here carry through the whole Centro-matic/South San Gabriel catalog.

label: Idol Records
description: Centro-matic's second album, recorded by Matt Pence at Jay Farrar's Illinois studio, thickens the fuzz-guitar rock of the debut with more developed arrangements while keeping Johnson's frayed, unpolished vocal delivery up front. Songs like 'Ruin This With Style' and 'This Vicious Crime' still sound cut live and fast, prioritizing feel over finish. It shows Centro-matic edging from lo-fi noise-rock toward the more country-inflected sound of their 2000s records.
lineage: Continues Centro-matic's fast, fuzz-heavy development toward the fuller alt-country/Crazy Horse sound of 'Distance and Clime' and 'Love You Just the Same'.

album: All the Falsest Hearts Can Try
label: Quality Park/Munich Records
description: Released the same year as 'Navigational' on the Netherlands-based Munich label, this album keeps pace with Centro-matic's rapid-fire recording habits of the late 1990s, another set of scuffed-up, guitar-forward rock songs built around Will Johnson's plainspoken drawl. It has the feel of a working band's second-tier output relative to their more celebrated 2000s records, but the same fuzzed, Crazy Horse-tilted core is already in place. It underlines how prolifically Centro-matic worked in their first Denton decade.
lineage: One of several parallel late-1990s Centro-matic releases that built up the fuzz-guitar, alt-country sound Denton, Texas bands would keep refining through the 2000s.
key_tracks: Cool That You Showed Us How

label: Idol/Munich
description: Centro-matic's fourth full-length pushes the band's fuzzed-out guitar rock into longer, more patient arrangements, trading some of the earlier records' scrappiness for a fuller, more deliberate sound. Will Johnson's songwriting stays plainspoken and drawled, but the band -- now a steadier four-piece with Scott Danbom and Mark Hedman -- plays with more room to stretch out. It sits at the midpoint between Centro-matic's lo-fi 1990s records and the more assured 'Love You Just the Same'.
lineage: Marks Centro-matic settling into its core lineup (Johnson, Pence, Danbom, Hedman), the same band that would carry through 'Love You Just the Same' and 'Fort Recovery'.

label: Misra/Munich
description: Widely considered one of Centro-matic's strongest records (it earned a rare 4-star AllMusic rating), 'Love You Just the Same' balances big, fuzzed-out guitar rockers like 'Mighty Midshipman' with quieter, more melodic turns. Will Johnson's voice is as ragged as ever, but the band's arrangements are tighter and more confident than on the 1990s records. It is a strong entry point for the Centro-matic side of the Molina/Magnolia orbit.
lineage: Represents the fully-formed, Denton-scene version of Centro-matic's Crazy Horse-indebted country rock, the direct sibling sound to Magnolia Electric Co.'s work of the same period.

label: Misra/Cooking Vinyl/Houston Party
description: Centro-matic's most widely reviewed album pairs some of the band's biggest, most anthemic guitar rock ('Covered Up in Mines', 'Patience for the Ride') with the same weathered, plainspoken vocals Johnson had carried since the mid-1990s. It got a UK release through Cooking Vinyl, broadening the band's reach beyond the American alt-country underground. It represents the commercial and critical peak of Centro-matic's main-band output.
lineage: The commercial high point of Centro-matic's Denton-scene guitar rock, released the same year as Magnolia Electric Co.'s parallel breakthrough records.

label: Misra/Cooking Vinyl/Houston Party
description: A double album pairing a disc of loud Centro-matic guitar rock with a disc of quieter South San Gabriel material, 'Dual Hawks' makes explicit that Will Johnson is the same songwriter running both projects at once. The Centro-matic half stays true to the band's fuzzed-out sound, while the South San Gabriel songs slow things down into hushed, pedal-steel-laced country-folk. Taken together it is the clearest single portrait of Johnson's split musical personality.
lineage: Unites Will Johnson's two parallel bands, Centro-matic (loud) and South San Gabriel (quiet), on one release, showing both halves of the Denton sound side by side.

label: Undertow Music Collective
description: Released on Will Johnson's own Undertow Music Collective imprint, Centro-matic's penultimate album keeps the band's guitar-forward rock intact while sounding more settled and self-assured than the earlier, scrappier records. It came in the same stretch of years as Johnson's Monsters of Folk and Molina and Johnson side projects, and carries some of that same weathered, well-worn songwriting. It is late-period Centro-matic: still loud, still drawled, a band comfortable in its own long-running sound.
lineage: Late-period Centro-matic, released on Will Johnson's own label as the band's Denton-scene run wound toward its 2014 finale.

album: Take Pride in Your Long Odds
label: Navigational Transmissions
description: Centro-matic's final album, released as the band called it quits after nearly two decades in Denton, wraps up their catalog of ragged, Crazy Horse-tilted guitar rock. It was self-released on Will Johnson's own Navigational Transmissions imprint rather than one of the band's earlier labels. As a farewell record it plays like a summation of the band's whole run, from lo-fi 1990s beginnings to the more assured songwriting of its later years.
lineage: Closes out Centro-matic's run as a band, the year after Jason Molina's death, marking the practical end of the classic Molina/Magnolia-era Denton-Bloomington-Chicago network.

label: Idol/Munich
description: Will Johnson's quieter alter-ego project to Centro-matic, South San Gabriel's debut was originally released under the Centro-matic name before Johnson split his catalog into a loud band and a hushed one. Sparse, slow, and largely acoustic, it points toward the slowcore-adjacent side of the Denton scene rather than Centro-matic's fuzzed-out rock. It is the origin point of a project Johnson would keep alive alongside Centro-matic for another decade.
lineage: Splits off from Centro-matic as Will Johnson's hushed, slow-tempo alter ego, establishing a quieter parallel track to the Crazy Horse fuzz of his main band.

album: The Carlton Chronicles: Not Until the Operation's Through
label: Misra/Munich/Houston Party
description: South San Gabriel's most fully-realized album pushes Will Johnson's quiet side project further into slowcore territory, all patient tempos, sparse arrangements, and pedal steel drones. It was written around the illness of a family member (the 'Carlton' of the title), giving the record a hushed, worried tone throughout. It is the clearest link between the Denton scene and the slowcore lineage that also runs through Low and Codeine.
lineage: Pushes Will Johnson's South San Gabriel project toward the slowcore lineage (Low, Codeine), a quieter sibling to both Centro-matic and the Magnolia Electric Co. sound.

label: Undertow
description: Will Johnson's first solo album, released while Centro-matic was still active, strips his songwriting down to just voice and acoustic guitar, closer to a demo tape than a full-band record. It is quieter and more intimate than either Centro-matic or South San Gabriel, letting his weathered, plainspoken vocal carry the whole record. It set the pattern for Johnson's parallel solo career alongside his main bands.
lineage: Opens Will Johnson's solo catalog, a stripped-down extension of the same Denton songwriting that fed Centro-matic and South San Gabriel.

label: Misra/Munich
description: Will Johnson's second solo record continues the quiet, plainspoken songwriting of 'Murder of Tides', with a little more instrumental color layered around the acoustic core. It is unhurried and downcast, closer in mood to South San Gabriel than to Centro-matic's guitar rock. It reinforces Johnson's status as one of the steadiest, most prolific songwriters in the Denton/Magnolia orbit.
lineage: Continues Will Johnson's stripped-down solo work alongside his ongoing Centro-matic and South San Gabriel output.
key_tracks: Just to Know What You've Been Dreaming

label: Keeled Scales
description: A later Will Johnson solo record, released well after Centro-matic's 2014 breakup, keeps the same plainspoken, acoustic-centered songwriting he has carried since 'Murder of Tides'. It is quieter and more reflective than his band records, the sound of a veteran Denton songwriter still working the same hushed, weathered vein two decades on. It extends the Molina/Magnolia circle's aftermath well past the lane's core years.
lineage: A post-Centro-matic Will Johnson solo record continuing the hushed, plainspoken songwriting he established in the Molina/Magnolia era.

label: Keeled Scales
description: Will Johnson's ninth solo album, covered by No Expectations as patient music with effortless hooks, leads with his weary voice and evocative lyrics over unhurried, largely acoustic arrangements. Coming fifty years into his career, it is the sound of the same Denton songwriter who started Centro-matic in 1995 still working the same plainspoken vein. It stands as the most recent chapter of the Molina/Magnolia-orbit story the assignment traces back to the mid-1990s.
lineage: The most recent entry in Will Johnson's solo catalog, extending the Centro-matic/South San Gabriel/Molina and Johnson lineage nearly thirty years on.

label: Thrill Jockey
description: Baltimore's Arbouretum plays slow, heavy, guitar-drenched folk-rock in an explicitly Crazy Horse-scale mode, with Dave Heumann's baritone drawl riding over extended, fuzzed-out solos. 'Rites of Uncovering' is the band's second album and first widely reviewed one, closer to stoner-rock heaviness than to the alt-country twang of Centro-matic, but sharing the same lineage of haunted, guitar-forward Americana as the Molina/Magnolia catalog. It plays like a doom-tinged cousin to Neil Young's own Crazy Horse records.
lineage: Extends the Neil Young/Crazy Horse guitar lineage that also runs through Magnolia Electric Co., pushing it toward heavier, stoner-rock-adjacent territory from Baltimore rather than the Midwest or Texas.

label: Thrill Jockey
description: Arbouretum's third album keeps the band's heavy, extended-jam approach to guitar rock but brings in strings and slightly more melodic songwriting on tracks like the title track and 'False Spring'. Dave Heumann's plainspoken baritone still anchors songs that stretch past five and six minutes, closer to a doom-folk take on Crazy Horse than to conventional alt-country. It is a strong mid-period entry in the band's catalog.
lineage: Continues Arbouretum's Crazy Horse-scale, heavy-guitar folk rock, the same lineage Molina and Neil Young himself sit at the root of.

label: Thrill Jockey
description: Named one of the year's best albums by both Mojo and Uncut, 'The Gathering' is Arbouretum's widest-reaching record, built on long, heavy guitar excursions like the ten-minute 'Song of the Nile' alongside a cover of Jimmy Webb's 'The Highwayman'. Dave Heumann's baritone stays plain and unhurried even as the guitars pile up into extended, distorted jams. It is the clearest 'Essential' entry point into Arbouretum's Crazy Horse-scale sound.
lineage: Arbouretum's critical peak, the fullest expression of the Baltimore band's Crazy Horse-indebted, heavy-guitar folk rock within the wider Molina/Magnolia-adjacent V1 lane.

label: Thrill Jockey
description: Arbouretum's fifth album keeps the band's slow, heavy guitar-rock formula intact on tracks like 'The Long Night' and 'Renouncer', with Dave Heumann's baritone as unhurried as ever over extended, distorted jams. It closes out the band's core 1996-2013-era run at the same volume and pace they had established since 'Rites of Uncovering'. Later albums ('Let It All In') would keep the sound going well past this record.
lineage: Closes Arbouretum's core lane-era run of Crazy Horse-scale Baltimore guitar rock, a sound the band would continue past 2013 largely unchanged.

label: Thrill Jockey
description: Released well past the lane's core years, Arbouretum's later album 'Let It All In' keeps the same slow, heavy guitar-rock sound the band established with 'Rites of Uncovering' over a decade earlier. Dave Heumann's baritone and the band's extended, fuzzed-out jams on tracks like 'A Prism in Reverse' show a band that has not changed its approach much since 2007. It is included here as a continuation of the same unbroken Crazy Horse-scale catalog rather than a new direction.
lineage: A 2020 continuation of Arbouretum's long-running Crazy Horse-scale sound, unchanged enough from their 2007-2013 records to belong with the rest of their V1 catalog.

album: Who Will Walk in the Darkness with You?
label: Delmore Recording Society
description: Columbus, Ohio's The Black Swans build a spare, haunted folk-rock sound around Jerry DeCicca's cracked, weary voice, with violinist Noel Sayre's playing giving the songs an eerie, mournful edge. The band's debut is slow and hushed throughout, closer to a graveside hymn than to a rock record, sharing the same Midwestern gothic-folk atmosphere as Songs: Ohia. It is Molina-adjacent in tone and geography without being directly connected to his bands.
lineage: A Columbus, Ohio band working the same haunted, Midwestern gothic-folk atmosphere as Jason Molina's Songs: Ohia, sharing scene and tone rather than direct collaboration.
key_tracks: Who Will Walk in the Darkness With You?

label: Merge Records
description: Butterglory's debut pairs Matt Suggs and Debby Vander Wall's dual, half-mumbled vocals with cheaply recorded, fuzzed-out guitar pop, alternating scrappy full-band tracks with four-track home recordings. It sounds like a Kansas cousin to early Pavement and Guided by Voices, more interested in melodic fragments than polish. Songs like 'Waiting on the Guns' and 'Cactus' show the band's knack for hooks buried under tape hiss.
lineage: Part of the Merge Records roster alongside Superchunk and the Karl Hendricks Trio, Butterglory brought Lawrence, Kansas's lo-fi scene into the same Matador/Merge slacker-rock conversation as Pavement and Guided by Voices.
